criteria.name: Mission concept and rationale — What will it do, who are the users, why is it needed?
criteria.reasoning: The concept, rationale and need (bleaching monitoring, near-real-time relay, SST, thermal stress, bathymetry) are clear and supported by footnoted sources. However, mission objectives and quantitative requirements (revisit, resolution, latency) are not specified, and users are essentially limited to scientists. Referencing is URL footnotes rather than a full reference list, and the acidification causal claim is loose.

evidence.quote: Hundreds of millions of humans rely on reefs for food, natural protection, jobs, and tourism.
A near-real-time relay to monitoring stations on the ground would allow marine and conservation scientists

criteria.name: Project plan — How you plan to complete the assignment, including either a Gantt chart or a timetable and information sources you plan to use
criteria.reasoning: A detailed weekly Gantt chart with deadlines and task descriptions makes the plan feasible-looking. However, no contingencies or variations are provided, information sources are only vaguely named, and the plan's text contradicts the chart on editing weeks. The orbit choice is technically unsound, which undermines confidence in the plan's grounding in the mission concept.

evidence.quote: Project work will be divided into weeks via a Gantt Chart.
Weeks 7 and 8 are reserved for review, amendments, final simulations, and reflection.
My current choice is a geostationary orbit at an altitude of 600 km

criteria.name: Preliminary progress — Technical content and evidence of sufficient work done to date
criteria.reasoning: Some work is evidenced (literature review, STK tutorials), but no technical results, calculations, orbit analysis or STK outputs are presented. The progress is minor and not interpreted, so it falls short of showing the design is on track.

evidence.quote: I have read the brief of Asner’s monitoring system in Hawaii

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Clear headings, consistent superscript footnotes and a readable Gantt chart are positives. Weaknesses include awkward phrasing, the chart is not formally captioned as a figure, the text and chart conflict on editing weeks, and references are URL footnotes rather than a reference list.

evidence.quote: Oceans have become 30 percent more acidic since the industrial revolution
Detailed task descriptions can be found on the next page.

technical_issues.where: Project Plan & Preliminary Progress – Orbit Specifics
technical_issues.issue: A geostationary orbit is at about 35,786 km and must be equatorial; 600 km is LEO. A GEO cannot remain fixed over the Great Barrier Reef (roughly 10–24°S).
Ocean acidification is stated as leading to coral bleaching. Bleaching is primarily driven by thermal stress, so the causal claim is incorrect or oversimplified.

technical_issues.where: Project Plan & Preliminary Progress – Editing & Finalisation
technical_issues.issue: Text says weeks 7 and 8 are for review and finalisation, but the Gantt chart schedules Editing & Finalisation in weeks 9–10.

overall: Good mission motivation and a usable Gantt chart, but the orbit choice is technically wrong (GEO at 600 km cannot hover over the reef), the plan has no contingencies or explicit sources, and preliminary technical results are minimal. Presentation is adequate with some inconsistencies.

feedback.summary: You have a clear and well-motivated concept. Your explanation of why reef monitoring matters, and of the value of a near-real-time relay to ground stations, is easy to follow. The main problem is the orbit: a geostationary orbit must be about 35,786 km above the equator, so it cannot hover over the Great Barrier Reef at 600 km. Fixing this, along with the plan inconsistency and the thin preliminary results, will raise your work considerably.
next_steps: Correct the orbit choice so it is technically valid and justify it against the reef's latitude and your coverage and latency needs. Also revise the bleaching explanation so it names thermal stress as the primary driver.
Make the project plan consistent: align the text on weeks 7 to 8 with the Gantt chart's weeks 9 to 10, and add contingencies for likely delays or design variations.
Present preliminary results for your corrected orbit, such as STK outputs with a short interpretation, and replace the URL footnotes with a full reference list.

criteria.C1: You clearly describe the mission concept and why reef monitoring matters, including the reef's value for food, protection, jobs and tourism. Your relay to ground stations is well motivated. To reach the higher level, define measurable objectives and requirements, such as revisit time, spatial resolution and data latency. Broaden your users beyond scientists to include reef managers and other decision-makers. Correct the bleaching claim, since thermal stress is the main driver, and use a full reference list.
criteria.C2: Your weekly Gantt chart with deadlines and task descriptions makes the plan look feasible. To reach the higher level, add contingencies and variations, and explain why the sequence suits the mission. Name your information sources specifically. Resolve the conflict between the text (weeks 7 and 8) and the chart (weeks 9 and 10). The orbit error also weakens the link between your plan and the mission concept.
criteria.C3: You have made progress: you completed STK tutorials 1 to 4 and reviewed the Asner Hawaii monitoring brief. However, no results, orbit analysis or STK outputs are yet presented or interpreted. Add preliminary results for your corrected orbit, such as ground tracks, coverage or pass-time outputs, with a brief interpretation of what they show about your design and whether you are on track.
criteria.C4: Your headings, consistent footnotes and readable Gantt chart give the report a clear structure. To reach the higher level, tighten the phrasing, which is sometimes awkward. Give the Gantt chart a formal figure caption and refer to it in the text. Fix the editing-week contradiction. Replace URL footnotes with a reference list that matches your in-text citations.
